opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I use it a lot, and honestly the way I use it has changed how I think about learning things.

The basic pattern is that whenever I get curious about something, whether it's a technical question, some piece of history, or a decision I'm trying to make, I'll just fire off a deep research query instead of going down a rabbit hole of twenty browser tabs myself. What used to take me an afternoon of reading, skimming, and trying to piece together what's credible now comes back in a few minutes as a pretty well-organized report with sources I can check.

One thing I've learned is that the quality of what you get back depends a lot on how you frame the question. If I just ask something vague, I get something generic. But if I tell it who I am, what I already know, and what I'm actually trying to figure out, like "I understand the basics here, I want to know where the experts disagree," the result is dramatically better. It's almost like briefing a really sharp research assistant.

I also use it as a starting point rather than an endpoint. I'll read the report, find the two or three threads that are actually interesting, and then go deeper on those, sometimes with follow-up queries, sometimes by reading the original sources it pointed me to. It's very good at giving me a map of a territory I didn't know, and then I decide where I want to walk.

And there's a bit of a meta reason I like it, too. Having spent so long thinking about where these models are going, using deep research is a pretty visceral reminder of what changes when you give a model more time to think and the ability to take actions, like searching, reading, and revising. It's not just answering from memory; it's actually doing work. That shift from chatbot to something that does real tasks for you is, I think, one of the most important things happening in AI right now, and deep research is one of the clearest early examples of it.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research can return a report in minutes for varied questions, but does not specifically say it answers scientific what-if questions in seconds or that those questions previously took weeks to investigate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I've found that deep research has really changed the way I satisfy curiosity. Before, if I got interested in something, say the history of some technology, or why some industry is structured the way it is, I'd do a few Google searches, read a Wikipedia article, maybe skim a couple of papers, and I'd get maybe sixty percent of the way to an answer. And then I'd kind of give up because getting the rest of the way required real effort.

Now what I do is I'll just write out the question, and I try to write it the way I'd write it to a smart grad student. Here's what I'm curious about, here's what I already know, here's the thing that confuses me. And then I let it go. It comes back fifteen, twenty minutes later with something that reads like a real briefing document, with sources I can actually check.

And the interesting thing is it's not really about the first answer. It's that the first answer generates five more questions. So I'll read it, and I'll think, wait, that doesn't quite square with this other thing I believed, and I'll ask a follow-up. I've spent whole evenings going down rabbit holes on things like the economics of shipping containers, or how a particular drug got discovered, just following the thread.

The thing I'd say to people is that the quality of what you get out is really determined by the quality of the question you put in. If you ask something vague, you get a vague, encyclopedic answer. If you ask something specific, with your actual confusion in it, you get something that feels like it was written for you. And honestly I think that's a skill people are going to need to develop, learning to articulate what you're actually curious about.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes getting a research briefing in fifteen or twenty minutes and exploring follow-up questions, but does not say it answers scientific what-if questions in seconds or that those questions previously took weeks to investigate.

astra-6.text:
I use it when I’m curious about something but don’t yet know enough to ask a really precise question. I’ll start broad: what are the main ideas here, what do people disagree about, and what evidence would help me understand that disagreement? Then I use the report to figure out where I want to go deeper.

The useful part is that it gives you a map of a subject. You can see connections you wouldn’t necessarily have known to search for. And then the follow-up questions become much more interesting. So for me, it’s less about getting one definitive answer and more about getting far enough into a topic that I can start asking better questions.

r001.rationale: The response describes using deep research to map a topic and develop better follow-up questions, but does not say it can answer scientific what-if questions in seconds instead of weeks.
